531.event_title: The Wall Street boom ends in the Crash of 1929
531.event: During the prosperous 1920s, share prices on the New York Stock Exchange rose to unprecedented heights, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average increasing about six-fold between 1921 and September 1929, and millions of ordinary people bought stocks, many with borrowed money while putting down only about a tenth of the price. In mid-October 1929 the prominent economist Irving Fisher said that stock prices appeared to have reached a permanently high plateau. Days later the market fell nearly 13 percent on 28 October and nearly 12 percent on 29 October, and by mid-November the Dow had lost almost half its value, a collapse that contributed to the Great Depression.
531.explanation: The long boom bred an optimism so complete that borrowing replaced caution and warnings were brushed aside, and the fall was all the harder for it.
531.tie_back: The kural warns that the carelessness born of great joy does more harm than even boundless anger, and the euphoria of the late 1920s led millions to drop their guard just before the crash.
531._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of heedlessness bred by the delight of great wealth, though it is a collective mood rather than one person's lapse.

532.place: Polo Grounds, New York City, United States
532.event: In a game tied 1-1 between the New York Giants and the Chicago Cubs, the Giants appeared to score the winning run in the bottom of the ninth inning on a single by Al Bridwell. Fred Merkle, the 19-year-old runner on first base, headed off the field without touching second base as fans poured onto the field, the Cubs' Johnny Evers claimed a force-out at second, and the umpire ruled Merkle out, so the game ended in a tie. The two teams finished the season level, the Cubs won the replayed game and the National League pennant, and Merkle, though he went on to play in five World Series, was mocked for years with nicknames such as Bonehead.
532.explanation: One moment of inattention by a capable player became the thing he was remembered for, overshadowing the rest of a long career.
532.tie_back: The kural says forgetfulness kills a person's good name, and one forgotten step to second base shaped Fred Merkle's reputation for the rest of his life.
532._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a single lapse of attention, not a lack of ability, destroyed a man's good name.

533.event_title: Henri Becquerel develops the plates he had put away
533.event: Henri Becquerel was testing whether uranium salts, after exposure to sunlight, gave off rays like the newly discovered X-rays, by placing the salts on photographic plates wrapped in black paper. When cloudy weather in late February 1896 interrupted the experiments, he stored the salts and wrapped plates together in a drawer, and on 1 March he developed the plates anyway and found clear images. Further tests showed that the uranium gave off penetrating rays without any sunlight, the discovery of radioactivity, for which he shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with Pierre and Marie Curie.
533.explanation: Becquerel's lasting fame rests on a careful check of plates that seemed unlikely to show anything at all.
533.tie_back: The kural says the heedless never win lasting fame, and Becquerel's enduring name shows the reverse: fame that came from refusing to overlook a small, apparently pointless step.
533._accuracy_note: Illustrates the kural from the positive side, attentiveness bringing fame, rather than showing heedlessness losing it; the kural's appeal to the agreement of all treatises has no direct parallel.

534.event_title: The Dutch raid on the Medway
534.event: During a war between England and the Dutch Republic, while peace talks were under way at Breda, much of the English fleet lay laid up in the River Medway near the royal dockyard at Chatham, above a defensive chain across the river. In June 1667 a Dutch fleet under Michiel de Ruyter took Sheerness, sailed up the Medway, broke through the chain, burned a number of English ships and towed away the English flagship Royal Charles, while the English sank some of their own large ships to block the channel. The raid put pressure on Charles II, and the Dutch obtained better terms in the Treaty of Breda.
534.explanation: England possessed one of the strongest navies of its day, yet ships left idle behind a weak boom could not protect even their own home dockyard.
534.tie_back: The kural says that just as no fortress helps the fearful, no advantage helps the heedless, and England's great warships were of no use while they lay unready in the Medway.
534._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a great advantage made useless by unreadiness; the sources describe the fleet as laid up rather than spelling out the decisions behind it.

535.event: The Vajont dam was built in a gorge known to be geologically unstable, and several geologists and engineers warned of the risk of a single great landslide if the reservoir were filled. When filling began in 1960 the slope of Monte Toc started to move, and in November 1960 a slide of about 700,000 cubic metres fell into the lake, but the reservoir continued to be operated and raised again. On the night of 9 October 1963 a vast landslide fell into the reservoir, sending a wave over the dam that destroyed the town of Longarone below and killed about 2,000 people, although the dam itself survived; several people involved were later convicted in the courts.
535.explanation: The warning signs were seen and measured for three years, but the danger was not guarded against while there was still time, and once the mountain moved nothing could be done.
535.tie_back: The kural says one who fails to guard against trouble before it comes will be left grieving over his own mistake once it strikes, and Vajont is remembered as a disaster foreseen but not prevented.
535._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural: a known, guardable danger neglected until it could only be mourned.

536.event_title: Walsingham's watchfulness uncovers the Babington Plot
536.event: Sir Francis Walsingham, secretary of state to Elizabeth I, kept a network of agents and informers to protect the queen. In 1586, learning through a double agent of a Catholic conspiracy, later named after Anthony Babington, to assassinate Elizabeth and put Mary, Queen of Scots, on the throne, Walsingham had Mary's secret letters, smuggled in beer barrels, intercepted, deciphered by his codebreaker Thomas Phelippes and resealed before delivery. The correspondence exposed the plot, and the conspirators were arrested and tried.
536.explanation: Watchfulness extended even to letters their writers thought secure protected the queen from a plot that might otherwise have succeeded.
536.tie_back: The kural says nothing equals unfailing watchfulness kept towards everyone and at all times, and Walsingham's constant vigilance is a classic example of it in statecraft.
536._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of sustained vigilance in government, though Walsingham's methods included manipulation that the kural does not address.

537.event_title: Amundsen sails the Gjoa through the Northwest Passage
537.place: Arctic waters of northern Canada, from Norway to Nome, Alaska
537.event: Many earlier expeditions had sought a sea route through the Arctic waters north of Canada without completing it. After careful preparation Roald Amundsen bought the small 47-ton sloop Gjoa, built in 1872, and left Kristiania (Oslo) on 16 June 1903 with six companions, spending two winters at Gjoa Haven on King William Island, where the party made magnetic observations, and a third winter near Herschel Island. The Gjoa reached Nome, Alaska, in August 1906, the first ship to sail the whole Northwest Passage.
537.explanation: A small, well-prepared party patiently completed over three years a voyage that larger and better-funded expeditions had failed to achieve.
537.tie_back: The kural says no task is too hard if it is done carefully with an unforgetting mind as one's tool, and Amundsen's methodical voyage conquered a route long thought impassable.
537._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of careful, persistent effort accomplishing a task long considered beyond reach.

538.event_title: Takaki Kanehiro's navy diet defeats beriberi
538.event: Beriberi was a major disease among Japanese sailors, and on one long voyage of the training ship Ryujo 169 of its 376 crew fell ill and 25 died. Naval surgeon Takaki Kanehiro, who believed the white-rice diet was to blame, had the ship Tsukuba sail a similar route in 1884 with a more varied diet, and only about 14 of its crew developed beriberi and none died, after which the navy changed its rations, adding barley, and beriberi in the navy fell sharply. The army, whose medical leaders doubted the dietary explanation, kept its white-rice ration, and in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-05 more than 27,000 army soldiers died of beriberi.
538.explanation: The navy acted on a well-tested remedy and was spared, while the army's neglect of the same lesson cost tens of thousands of lives.
538.tie_back: The kural warns that there is no good for those who neglect and leave undone what the wise have shown to be right, and the contrast between Japan's navy and army is a stark example.
538._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of neglecting proven good practice; Takaki's own explanation (lack of protein) was later shown to be incomplete, though his remedy worked.

539.event_title: Scipio Aemilianus foresees Rome's own fall at Carthage
539.event: In 146 BCE, at the end of the Third Punic War, the Roman commander Scipio Aemilianus captured and destroyed Carthage, Rome's great rival. The historian Polybius, who stood beside him, recorded that as Scipio watched the city's fall he took Polybius by the hand and said he felt a dread foreboding that the same fate might one day come to his own country. The later historian Appian wrote that Scipio wept as he looked on the city.
539.explanation: At the very height of Roman triumph, the victorious general turned his thoughts to how great powers fall rather than to his own glory.
539.tie_back: The kural tells those who feel strong and elated to remember others who were ruined, and Scipio did exactly that in the hour of his greatest victory.
539._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's advice to recall the fallen in the moment of success; the kural stresses heedlessness as the cause of ruin, which Scipio's remark leaves implicit.

540.event_title: Howard Carter's last season in the Valley of the Kings
540.place: Valley of the Kings, Luxor, Egypt
540.event: The archaeologist Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, had searched the Valley of the Kings for several seasons from 1917 with little to show for it, and in 1922 Carnarvon agreed to pay for one more season. On 4 November 1922, only days after work resumed, Carter's team uncovered a step cut into the rock, and further digging revealed a stairway leading down to a sealed doorway. It was the almost intact tomb of the pharaoh Tutankhamun, into which Carter and Carnarvon first looked on 26 November 1922.
540.explanation: Years of fruitless searching ended in one of the most famous archaeological discoveries ever made, because the searcher kept his goal in view when others were ready to stop.
540.tie_back: The kural says reaching what you have set your mind on is easy if you keep thinking of it steadily, and Carter's refusal to let go of his search in the Valley of the Kings was rewarded.
540._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of sustained focus on a goal; the role of luck and of Carnarvon's funding means it is not purely a matter of steady thought.
